parts.solution_md:
The electronic configurations of Cu and Cu<sup>2+ </sup>are:

- Cu: ([Ar]) 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Cu<sup>2+</sup>: ([Ar]) 3d<sup>9</sup>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Copper has 29 electrons*
- *Remember: **The 4s subshell is filled with electrons before the 3d subshell *
- *You would expect the electronic configuration to be [Ar]) 3d*<sup>*9 *</sup>*4s*<sup>*2 *</sup>*but a full 3d subshell is energetically favoured resulting in ([Ar]) 3d*<sup>*10*</sup>* 4s*<sup>*1*</sup>
- *To form a positive ion with a 2+ charge, two electrons are lost*

  - *One is removed from the 4s subshell first, and then one from the 3d subshell *

parts.problem_md:
A sample of copper contains the isotopes <sup>63</sup>Cu and <sup>65</sup>Cu.

i) Complete the table to show the numbers of subatomic particles in the atoms of these two isotopes of copper.

**(2)**

| **Isotope** | **Protons** | **Neutrons** | **Electrons** |
|---|---|---|---|
| <sup>63</sup>Cu |   |   |   |
| <sup>65</sup>Cu |   |   |   |

ii) Explain the term isotopes, using the information in the table.

**(2)**

iii) State why the two isotopes of copper have the same chemical reactions.

**(1)**

iv) The relative atomic mass of copper in this sample is 63.4. Calculate the percentage abundances of the isotopes <sup>63</sup>Cu and <sup>65</sup>Cu in this sample. 
You** must** show your working.

**(2)**
parts.solution_md:
i) The completed table is:

| **Isotope** | **Protons** | **Neutrons** | **Electrons** |
|---|---|---|---|
| <sup>63</sup>Cu | **29** | **34** | **29** |
| <sup>65</sup>Cu | **29** | **36** | **29** |

- Each correct row: **[1 mark]**
- Four or five correct; **1 mark]**

ii) The term isotope means:

- (Atoms / elements that have) same number of protons / same proton number / quoted same number of protons even if wrong; **[1 mark]**
- (But) different numbers of neutrons / neutron number; **[1 mark]**

iii) Two isotopes of copper have the same chemical reactions because:

- (Isotopes have) the same electronic configuration
**OR**
Same number of electrons
**OR**
Same electron arrangement; **[1 mark]**

iv) The percentage abundances of the isotopes <sup>63</sup>Cu and <sup>65</sup>Cu in this sample are:

- Expression relating isotopic masses *A*<sub>r</sub> and X  `63.4 space equals space fraction numerator open parentheses open parentheses 1 minus straight X close parentheses space cross times space 65 close parentheses space plus space open parentheses straight X space cross times space 63 close parentheses over denominator 1 end fraction`; **[1 mark]**
- Abundance of (Cu) 63 = 0.8 or 80%  
**AND** 
Abundance of (Cu) 65 = 0.2 or 20%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *You can use a Periodic Table to find the atomic number for copper which is 29*

  - *The atomic number is the number of protons so there are 29 protons in each isotope*
  - *In an atom, the number of protons and electrons are equal so there are 29 electrons in each isotope*
  - *Take the atomic number away from the mass number for each isotope to deduce the number of neutrons *
- *Remember: **Chemical properties are determined by the number of electrons in the outer shell so if there are the same number of electrons, the isotopes will react in the same way*
- *Part iv) requires manipulation of the equation used to calculate RAM:*

  - `fraction numerator open parentheses abundance space of space isotope space straight x space mass close parentheses plus open parentheses abundance space of space isotope space straight x space mass close parentheses over denominator 100 end fraction`
- *There are many ways this calculation can be done so a correct answer with no workings scores 2 marks*
- *An alternative method is:*

  - $63.4=\frac{(100-X)\times65)+(X\times63)}{100}$
  - *6340 = 6500 – 65X + 63X*
  - *6340 = 6500 – 2X*
  - *−160 = −2X*
  - *X **OR **63 = 80%*

parts.problem_md:
Copper(II) sulfate, CuSO<sub>4</sub>, can be made by reacting solid copper(II) carbonate with dilute sulfuric acid.

i) Write an equation for the reaction that occurs. State symbols are not required.

**(1)**

ii) An experiment was carried out to produce pure, dry crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO<sub>4</sub> •5H<sub>2</sub>O. 
Copper(II) carbonate was mixed with 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.00 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> sulfuric acid until no more reacted. The mass of CuSO<sub>4</sub> •5H<sub>2</sub>O obtained was 10.87g.

Calculate the percentage yield for this reaction, giving your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
[Molar mass of CuSO<sub>4</sub> •5H<sub>2</sub>O = 249.6 g mol<sup>−1</sup> ]

**(4)**
parts.solution_md:
i) An equation for the reaction that occurs is:

- CuCO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → CuSO<sub>4 </sub>+ CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O 
**OR** CuCO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) The percentage yield for this reaction, giving your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures is:

- Moles of sulfuric acid 50 × 1.00 ÷ 1000 = 0.05 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Maximum mass of copper(II) sulfate 0.05 (mol) × 249.6 = 12.48 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Percentage yield calculation: 100 × 10.87 ÷ 12.48 = 87.099; **[1 mark]**
- Answer to 2 or 3 SF 87(%) / 87.1(%); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Remember: **The general equation for the reaction between a metal carbonate and acid is:*

  - *Metal carbonate + acid     →    salt + water + carbon dioxide*
- *The equations required to answer part ii) are:*

  - *Number of moles = concentration x volume*
  
    - *Don't forget to convert the volume into dm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *Mass = molar mass x number of moles*
  
    - *The ratio of moles of sulfuric acid to copper sulfate is 1:1 so the number of moles of each substance is equal *
  - *Percentage yield = *$\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}\times100$
  - *If you don't give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures, you will not score the last mark *
  
    - *Two or three significant figures are considered appropriate *
- *An alternative method for ii) is:*

  - *Moles of sulfuric acid: 50 × 1.00 ÷ 1000 = 0.05 (mol)*
  - *Moles of copper sulfate:  10.87 (g) /: 249.6 (g) = 0.04355 (mol)*
  - *Percentage yield calculation: 100 × 0.04355 ÷ 0.05*
  - *Answer to 2 or 3 SF: 87(%) / 87.1(%)*
- *Marking point 4 can still be achieved even if the answer is incorrect as long as the calculation involves mass or moles*

equations.alt: fraction numerator actual space yield over denominator theoretical space yield end fraction cross times 100

parts.problem_md: Which equation represents the **second** ionisation energy of chlorine?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The second ionisation energy of chlorine is the energy taken to remove one mole** **of electrons from one mole of gaseous 1+ ions to form one mole of gaseous 2+ ions
- This can be shown by the equation:

  - Cl<sup>+</sup> (g) → Cl<sup>2+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>

**A** is incorrect as  the equation represents an electron is added to an ion rather than being removed

**B** is incorrect as  the equation represents electrons being added to an atom

**C** is incorrect as  one electron is being removed from each of two atoms

parts.problem_md: Which equation represents the **second** ionisation energy of magnesium?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The second ionisation energy of magnesium is represented by the removal of an electron from the 1+ ion / Mg<sup>+</sup> to form the 2+ ion / Mg<sup>2+</sup>, with both ions in the gaseous state

  - Mg<sup>+ </sup>(g) → Mg<sup>2+ </sup>(g) + e<sup>−</sup>

**A** is incorrect as  this represents the first and second ionisations

**C** is incorrect as  this represents the first and second ionisations **AND **the state symbols are incorrect

**D** is incorrect as  the state symbols are incorrect

parts.problem_md:
Several factors may affect ionisation energies:

I) the number of protons increases

II) the outer electron is further from the nucleus

III) the amount of shielding increases

IV) the number of unpaired outer electrons increases

Which factors explain the **decrease** in ionisation energy as Group 1 is descended?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Going down Group 1 the number of shells increases meaning the outer electron is further away from the nucleus
- With the increase in shells, there will also be more shielding from inner electrons
- Both factors will cause a decrease in the attraction between the outer electron and the nucleus resulting in less energy needed to remove it hence a lower ionisation energy

**A** and **C** are incorrect as  these are not reasons for decreasing ionisation energy down the group

** D** is incorrect as  I and IV are not reasons for decreasing ionisation energy down the group

parts.problem_md:
The graph shows log (ionisation energy) against ionisation number for the successive ionisations of an element.

![q5-paper-1-june-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](assets/001-q5-paper-1-june-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

In this element, how many quantum shells contain electrons, and how many electrons are in the outer quantum shell?

|   | ** ** | **Number of quantum shells** **containing electrons** | **Number of electrons in the** **outer quantum shell** |
|---|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **A** | 3 | 2 |
| ☐ | **B** | 3 | 5 |
| ☐ | **C** | 5 | 2 |
| ☐ | **D** | 5 | 5 |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- There are 3 quantum shells

  - This is indicated by the 2 large jumps between ionisation numbers 5 - 6 and 13 - 14
- There are 5 outer electrons

  - This is indicated by the first 5 points plotted / ionisation energies before the large jump between ionisation numbers 5 - 6
- An alternative method to answer this question would be to count up the number of ionisation numbers = 15

  - Look up element number 15 on the Periodic Table = phosphorus
  - Use that information to determine the number of quantum shells and outer electrons

**A** is incorrect as the outer five electrons require the least amount of energy to remove

**C** is incorrect as  there are two large jumps between the 3 quantum shells and the outer five electrons require the least amount of energy to remove

**D** is incorrect as there are two large jumps between the 3 quantum shells

parts.problem_md:
A stable ion, **M**<sup>**3+**</sup>, contains 18 electrons.

In which block of the Periodic Table is element **M** found?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- If an ion of **M** has a 3+ charge and 18 electrons, this means it has lost 3 electrons, so an atom of **M** must have 3 + 18 = 21 electrons
- Elements can form stable 3+ ions if they are either in Group 3 (i.e. the p block) or they are a transition element (i.e. in block d)
- No p block elements have 21 electrons, so it must be from the d block

**A** is incorrect as the s block elements don’t form stable 3+ ions

**B** is incorrect as  the elements which form stable 3+ ions do not have 21 electrons

**D** is incorrect as elements in the f block have more than 21 electrons

parts.problem_md: Which ion has the electronic configuration 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup> in its ground state?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Chlorine is in Period 3, along with sodium and aluminium

  - This rules out nitrogen
- Chlorine is in the p-block, along with aluminium

  - This rules out sodium
- Aluminium will lose three electrons to form the Al<sup>3+</sup> ion and gain a complete outer quantum shell

  - This results in the electron configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>
  - This rules aluminium out
- Chlorine will gain one electron to form the Cl<sup>–</sup> ion and gain a complete outer quantum shell

  - This results in the electron configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup>

**A** is incorrect as  Al<sup>3+</sup> has electronic configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>

**C** is incorrect as  N<sup>3−</sup> has electronic configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>

**D** is incorrect as  Na<sup>+</sup> has electronic configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>

parts.problem_md:
A p-block element in **Period 3 **of the Periodic Table reacts to form an ionic compound.

What could be the electronic configuration of the **ion **formed by this element?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- When forming an ion, a p-block element in Period 3 will either lose its outer s and p electrons to gain the electronic configuration of neon or gain p electrons to gain the electronic configuration of argon
- 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6 </sup>is the electronic configuration of argon, so could be the electronic configuration of a Period 3 p-block element

**A** is incorrect as  this is the electronic configuration of an s-block element

**C** is incorrect as  this could not be the electronic configuration of the ion of a p-block element

**D** is incorrect as  this could not be the electronic configuration of the ion of a Period 3 element
